A favorite of mine is Promising Young Woman. At first it’s about a woman coping with the loss of her best friend and the loss of her career. She’s tricking men at night to teach them a lesson, to cope with the reason why her friend killed herself. Then we meet her boss and Bo Burnham and you start to think she has a friend, plus she might fall in love. You have hope for her. She seems like she’s getting better. But then the plot thickens and she shifts to hardcore revenge. And instead of the new love story, Bo Burnham it turns out was there on the night her best friend was assaulted and saw everything. The shift from love story and hope, to deep revenge is heartbreaking. Every scene is beautiful. But when the mood changes, and she attacks the truck to the Liebestod from the opera Tristan und Isolde, it’s spellbinding.

Parasite fits this description. The first half is a comedy but as the story unfolds it takes a dark turn. 

Blue Collar is a movie I watched this year and I loved it. There isn’t a moment when the turn happens, it just kind of creeps up on you. I can’t really make sense of my favorite scene in the movie which is when the guys attend the party in the beginning. Seemed out of left field but there must have been a reason for it, but what a great movie.

How about Jaws (1975)? It spends the first half being a fairly standard (albeit brilliant) horror movie with an increasingly terrorised community, corrupt community leaders, and a series of innocent victims being finished off by the monster. The sense of fear established in the first half is carried over to the second, but the tone shifts from straight-forward horror to en exciting action/adventure story as the three men attempt to hunt and kill the monster. We get new elements in the iconic Williams score - a kind of jaunty, upbeat adventure theme that sounds almost joyful. The film also takes on, in the second half, a kind of Melvillesque, fatalistic tone as man and beast go 1to1 to the inevitable annihilation of either one or the other. If I was feeling pretentious I might say it shifts from a political narrative to an existential one.

Do yourself a favor, watch A Night To Remember. Titanic lifted from that film which is easily the best movie about that tragic voyage.

I assume you’re not talking genre switch-ups (like From Dusk Till Dawn) or movies that are darker than expected but still pretty tonally consistent (Heathers) or movies that just have seemingly dissonant halves but which build on the same themes (Full Metal Jacket)

So here’s my list:

Shallow Grave

Trainspotting

Boogie Nights

Magic Mike

Goodfellas

Several Coen Brothers movies (Fargo, Miller’s Crossing in particular) 

All of the above start off fairly lighthearted/comedic/entertaining and then have a distinctly grimmer second half

Blue Velvet (still has a weird tone early on, but it starts as typical suburban drama/film noir and just gets sicker and sicker as it goes on)

(Notamoviebut) “Mac Finds His Pride” from Its Always Sunny (goes from a typical cynical but funny episode of the show to something really beautiful and heartbreaking) 

Irreversible (the most vile kind of French cinema to a pretty mundane/sweet second half—which only makes the first half more brutal in retrospect)

Oldboy (slick and cool revenge thriller turns into sick parody of the genre) 

The Sixth Sense (chilling horror film turns into uplifting/sentimental drama) 

You’re Next (from eerie horror to broad “splatstick” comedy) 

Surprisingly Click gets really weird and dark

The Truman Show (funny dark comic satire to extremely cathartic, heartbreaking and ultimately uplifting drama) 

Synecdoche New York and Being John Malkovich both go from surrealist cringe comedy to the most existentially disturbing/frightening/depressing movies in the world

Not a great film necessarily, but I always thought Doctor Strange might have a good tonal shift if you skipped the opening scene where the bad guys steal the book, and then the scene where they read the book. I do find The Prestige to be a great film and it has a similar shift. It's not as extreme or explicit as in Doctor Strange, but it definitely changed the feel of the movie, not in a negative way nor markedly positive way for me, but I imagine it could be divisive especially if the movie didn't already stand firmly on its other merits by that point.

When it was released there was talk that Tarantino directed the first half and Robert Rodriguez directed the second half. The guilds have rules about how movies can be credited. For years you couldn't credit two directors on one film. This was a problem for the Coen brothers, so one would take a writing credit while the other took the directing credit even though they'd both work together on writing and directing the movies. This rule has since changed but I don't recall when. It must have been before No Country For Old Men because I think they both won best director for that one.

Excellent recommendation. That hard cut to the room the next day is the cinematic equivalent of a bucket of ice water right in the face. The film literally confronts the audience’s complicity for the first half of the movie: *You thought this was all fun and games? Think again.* Brilliant filmmaking.

“Sunshine” is curious because it turns into a different genre in the second half and feels slightly abrupt. But I read the shooting script and there’s all these amazing ideas about man’s relationship to God and the universe as a spiritual realm which really unified why Pinbacker was in the story and his motivations as to stopping the crew from succeeding. Problem was all those ideas are in *the descriptions* and not in dialog or action. I remember reading it and thinking ‘This isn’t going to translate.’ And, of course, it didn’t.
